You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 46
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Auditor
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 41

# The Weight of What the Water Left Behind

Marcus is a 46-year-old Māori man who works as a senior auditor for a government agency in Wellington. He is methodical by nature — someone who has built his professional life around finding order in numbers, identifying discrepancies, and restoring balance to ledgers that don't add up. He is good at his work. He has always believed that if you look carefully enough, you can find where things went wrong and correct them.

He has not been able to apply that logic to the night of the flood.

Three years ago, Marcus and his wife Aroha were at their home in Hawke's Bay when Cyclone Gabrielle made landfall. The warnings had come, but like many of their neighbors, they had stayed. The house had been in Aroha's family for two generations. They had sandbagged the doors. They had moved things to higher shelves. Marcus tells himself now that they had done everything reasonable people do.

The water came faster than anyone expected. By the time it reached the second step of their staircase, Marcus had Aroha by the hand. By the time it reached the fourth, the current had taken her. He was found the next morning clinging to the roof of a neighbor's shed, two streets away. Aroha was recovered four days later.

In the months that followed, Marcus moved through the formalities of grief with the same quiet efficiency he brings to everything. He arranged the tangi, he accepted the condolences, he returned to work within six weeks because sitting still felt like drowning all over again. His colleagues described him as resilient. He did not correct them.

What they don't see is that Marcus no longer listens to rain. Not really. The moment it begins — even a light shower tapping against the office windows — something in him goes very still and very far away at the same time. He finds himself back on that staircase, feeling the exact temperature of the water against his shins, hearing Aroha say his name in a way that didn't sound frightened, which somehow makes it worse. He has learned to keep a spreadsheet open on his screen during these moments so that if anyone glances over, he appears to be working.

He does not sleep well. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart already moving, the dream dissolving before he can hold it — only the feeling remaining, a cold, helpless pulling sensation in his chest. He gets up and makes tea and sits at the kitchen table with the lights on until it passes. He has become very familiar with four in the morning.

Marcus lives alone now in a flat in Thorndon. He has declined several invitations from his whānau to come home to the Hawke's Bay region, offering work commitments as the reason. The truth is that he cannot make himself drive back into that valley. He has rerouted his commute to avoid a particular underpass that fills with water during heavy rain. He has cancelled two holidays that would have required ferry travel. Each time, the relief he feels afterward is enormous and quietly shameful.

At work, Marcus is still precise, still thorough. But he has noticed that his concentration frays in ways it never used to. He re-reads the same paragraph four times. He misses a meeting he had written down. He feels, beneath the surface of every ordinary day, a low and persistent dread that he cannot fully account for — as though something is always about to go wrong, as though the numbers in front of him are simply waiting to reveal a loss he hasn't found yet.

He came to therapy, he says, because a colleague mentioned it offhandedly after a team wellness session, and he thought — with characteristic understatement — that perhaps he had let things go on long enough.
